why_not.en: The action kostet slid to the end. That's how the tail of a long sentence after "that" or "because" sounds; in a simple sentence kostet is car #2.

why.why_voice_en: One thing — kostet. Sonst noch etwas? is the seller's ready-made phrase; learn it as one piece.

ch06_d6_04.en: No, thanks. I'll take the fish.

why.text_en: Nein, danke is a polite "no" and takes no place. The fish is being taken — the "what" car, so den Fisch.
why.why_de_en: The article signals the role: der → den/einen marks the "what" (the object): Ich nehme den Fisch.
why.why_en: Like English he → him, the role changes the form. In German the article changes: der Fisch → Ich nehme den Fisch.

why_not.en: English habit: "the" never changes. A German hears the wrong role: here the der-word is the "what" (object), so it's den.

why.text_en: Bitte schön without a question means "You're welcome". Auf Wiedersehen — a polite goodbye.
why.why_de_en: Two ready-made formulas in a row: Bitte schön + Auf Wiedersehen. Learn each as one piece; there's no action, so there's no train.
why.why_en: Like English "You're welcome. Goodbye!" — two fixed pieces: Bitte schön. Auf Wiedersehen!

why_not.en: The mistake is gluing it all together and translating word by word. These are 2 pieces; learn each whole: Bitte schön · Auf Wiedersehen.

why.root_en: Wiedersehen = wieder + sehen (wieder — again; sehen — to see), like "see you again" — Wiktionary
